Chapter 1 · History · India and the Contemporary World II

The Rise of Nationalism in Europe

Nationalism brought Europe’s peoples together and tore its empires apart. This chapter follows the idea from the French Revolution through liberalism and 1848, the unifications of Germany and Italy, Britain’s very different path, and the visual language of Marianne and Germania.

Chapter Overview

What this chapter is about, at a glance

In 1848, Frédéric Sorrieu, a French artist, prepared a series of four prints visualising his dream of a world made up of “democratic and social Republics”. Peoples of Europe and America — the United States and Switzerland ahead, then France with the revolutionary tricolour, then Germany with a black-red-gold flag, then Austria, Poland, Hungary — march in a long train past the Statue of Liberty, offering homage as they pass, while on the earth lie the shattered remains of the symbols of absolutist institutions. In Sorrieu’s utopian vision, the peoples of the world are grouped as distinct nations, identified through their flags and national costume.

The chapter then traces how that dream was actually made. The French Revolution of 1789 introduced the ideas of la patrie and le citoyen, the tricolour, uniform laws and a common language, and it produced the first clear expression of nationalism. The nation-state — a state in which the majority of its citizens, and not only its rulers, came to develop a sense of common identity and shared history or descent — became the goal, and Ernst Renan asked what a nation really is.

Through the nineteenth century the idea advanced unevenly: the liberal middle classes and the Zollverein, the conservative settlement of Vienna in 1815, the revolutions of 1830 and 1848 and the Frankfurt Parliament, Germany’s unification by Bismarck’s “blood and iron”, Italy’s long struggle from Mazzini’s Young Italy through Cavour’s diplomacy to Garibaldi’s Red Shirts, and Britain’s slow, parliamentary and sometimes repressive making of a United Kingdom.

The last sections turn to the visual language of nationalism — Marianne, Germania and the Statue of Liberty — and to its dark side: the Balkans after 1871, where nationalism became competitive and imperial, and where the First World War would begin.

Nation-state

A state in which the majority of its citizens, and not only its rulers, come to develop a sense of common identity and shared history or descent.

Nationalism

A sense of collective identity and belonging to a nation, forged through shared history, language, culture and symbols.

Absolutist

A government or system of rule that has no restraints on the power exercised — a form of monarchical government that was centralised, militarised and repressive.

Utopian

A vision of a society that is so ideal that it is unlikely to actually exist.

Plebiscite

A direct vote by which all the people of a region are asked to accept or reject a proposal.

Liberalism

Derived from the Latin root liber, meaning free — for the new middle classes it stood for freedom for the individual and equality of all before the law; politically it meant government by consent, and economically freedom of markets.

Suffrage

The right to vote.

Conservatism

A political philosophy that stressed the importance of tradition, established institutions and customs, and preferred gradual development to quick change.

Zollverein

The customs union formed in 1834 at Prussia’s initiative, which abolished tariff barriers and reduced the number of currencies from over thirty to two.

Allegory

A story, poem or image with a hidden meaning — usually a moral or political one; in nationalist art, a female figure standing for the nation.

Plebiscite and referendum

A plebiscite is a direct vote by all the people of a region on a proposal; a referendum is a general vote on a single political question.

Junkers

Large landowners of Prussia, who dominated the united Germany’s army and bureaucracy.

Romanticism

A cultural movement which sought to develop a particular form of nationalist sentiment by criticising the glorification of reason and science and focusing on emotions, intuition and mystical feelings.

Ethnic

Relating to a common racial, tribal or cultural origin or background that a community identifies with or claims.

Frédéric Sorrieu’s Dream and the Idea of the Nation-State

In 1848, Frédéric Sorrieu, a French artist, prepared a series of four prints visualising his dream of a world made up of “democratic and social Republics”. The first print shows the peoples of Europe and America — men and women of all ages and social classes — marching in a long train, offering homage to the Statue of Liberty as they pass it. Liberty is personified as a female figure — the torch of Enlightenment in one hand and the Charter of the Rights of Man in the other.

On the earth in the foreground lie the shattered remains of the symbols of absolutist institutions. In Sorrieu’s utopian vision, the peoples of the world are grouped as distinct nations, identified through their flags and national costume. Leading the procession, way past the statue, are the peoples of Europe and America — the United States and Switzerland lead the way, followed by France, identifiable by the revolutionary tricolour, having just reached the statue; behind France is the peoples of Germany carrying a black-red-gold flag; then follow the peoples of Austria, Poland, Hungary and other nations, holding aloft their respective flags.

Definition

Utopian: a vision of a society that is so ideal that it is unlikely to actually exist. Sorrieu’s prints are utopian — a dream of what Europe might become, not a description of what it was.

During the nineteenth century, nationalism emerged as a force which brought about sweeping changes in the political and mental world of Europe, and the end result was the emergence of the nation-state.

Definition

Nation-state: a state in which the majority of its citizens, and not only its rulers, came to develop a sense of common identity and shared history or descent. This commonness did not exist from time immemorial — it was forged through struggles, through the actions of leaders and the common people.

The French Revolution and the Idea of the Nation

The first clear expression of nationalism came with the French Revolution in 1789. France was a full-fledged territorial state in 1789 under the rule of an absolute monarch, and the political and constitutional changes that came in the wake of the Revolution led to the transfer of sovereignty from the monarchy to a body of French citizens. The revolution proclaimed that it was the people who would henceforth constitute the nation and shape its destiny.

From the very beginning, the French revolutionaries introduced various measures and practices that could create a sense of collective identity amongst the French people:

  • The ideas of la patrie (the fatherland) and le citoyen (the citizen) emphasised the notion of a united community enjoying equal rights under a constitution.
  • A new French flag, the tricolour, was chosen to replace the former royal standard.
  • The Estates General was elected by the body of active citizens and renamed the National Assembly.
  • New hymns were composed, oaths taken and martyrs commemorated, all in the name of the nation.
  • A centralised administrative system was put in place and it formulated uniform laws for all citizens within its territory.
  • Internal customs duties and dues were abolished and a uniform system of weights and measures was adopted.
  • Regional dialects were discouraged and French, as it was spoken and written in Paris, became the common language of the nation.

The revolutionaries further declared that it was the mission and destiny of the French nation to liberate the peoples of Europe from despotism — in other words, to help other peoples of Europe to become nations. When the news of the events in France reached the different cities of Europe, students and other members of educated middle classes began setting up Jacobin clubs, and their activities and campaigns prepared the way for the French armies which moved into Holland, Belgium, Switzerland and much of Italy in the 1790s. With the outbreak of the revolutionary wars, the French armies began to carry the idea of nationalism abroad.

Within the wide swathe of territory that came under his control, Napoleon set about introducing many of the reforms that he had already introduced in France. Through a return to monarchy Napoleon had, no doubt, destroyed democracy in France, but in the administrative field he had incorporated revolutionary principles in order to make the whole system more rational and efficient:

  • The Civil Code of 1804 — usually known as the Napoleonic Code — did away with all privileges based on birth, established equality before the law and secured the right to property.
  • He simplified administrative divisions, abolished the feudal system and freed peasants from serfdom and manorial dues.
  • In towns guild restrictions were removed, transport and communication systems were improved, and peasants, artisans, workers and new businessmen enjoyed a new-found freedom.
  • Businessmen and small-scale producers of goods realised that uniform laws, standardised weights and measures and a common national currency would facilitate the movement and exchange of goods and capital from one region to another.

But the initial enthusiasm soon turned to hostility, as it became clear that the new administrative arrangements did not go hand in hand with political freedom. Increased taxation, censorship, forced conscription into the French armies required to conquer the rest of Europe — all these seemed to outweigh the advantages of the administrative changes.

What Is a Nation? Ernst Renan’s Answer

In a lecture at the Sorbonne in 1882, the French philosopher Ernst Renan asked: what is a nation? His answer was influential and has been used to define a nation ever since.

Source extract

“A nation is the culmination of a long past of endeavours, sacrifice and devotion. A heroic past, great men, glory, that is the social capital upon which one bases a national idea. To have common glories in the past, to have a common will in the present, to have performed great deeds together, to wish to perform still more — these are the essential conditions of being a people. A nation is therefore a large-scale solidarity… Its existence is a daily plebiscite… A province is its inhabitants; if anyone has the right to be consulted, it is the inhabitant. A nation never has any real interest in annexing or holding on to a country against its will. The existence of nations is a good thing, a necessity even. Their existence is a guarantee of liberty, which would be lost if the world had only one law and only one master.”

Renan’s point is that a nation is not a fixed, ancient thing — it is made by shared memory and present-day consent, a “daily plebiscite”. Nations are not eternal: they had a beginning and may end, and their existence is a guarantee of liberty against a single master.

The Making of Nationalism — the Aristocracy, the Middle Class and Liberalism

Some of the changes that produced nationalism were economic and social. There were no nation-states as we know them in mid-eighteenth-century Europe: Germany, Italy and Switzerland were divided into kingdoms, duchies and cantons whose rulers had their autonomous territories; eastern and central Europe were under autocratic monarchies within which lived peoples speaking different languages. They did not share a collective identity or a common culture; they often spoke different languages and belonged to different ethnic groups — the Habsburg Empire, for instance, ruled over Austria-Hungary, a patchwork of many different regions and peoples, including Alpine regions, the Bohemian nobility, the Sudetenland and the provinces of Lombardy and Venetia — and such differences did not easily promote a sense of political unity.

The aristocracy and the new middle class

The aristocracy was the dominant class on the continent, united by a common way of life across regions — owning estates in the countryside and town houses. But their numbers were small. The majority of the population was made up of peasantry. Industrialisation, however, brought into being a new middle class comprising industrialists, businessmen and professionals. In Western and parts of Central Europe the growth of industrial production and trade meant the growth of towns and the emergence of commercial classes whose existence was based on production for the market. In Central and Eastern Europe these groups were smaller in number till late nineteenth century, and it was among the educated, liberal middle classes that ideas of national unity following the abolition of aristocratic privileges gained popularity.

Liberalism

The term “liberalism” derives from the Latin root liber, meaning free. For the new middle classes it stood for freedom for the individual and equality of all before the law. Politically, it emphasised the concept of government by consent, and revolutionaries in France were inspired by it. Yet equality before the law did not necessarily stand for universal suffrage: in revolutionary France, which marked the first political experiment in liberal democracy, the right to vote and to get elected was granted exclusively to property-owning men. Men without property and all women were excluded. It was only through the political and social upheavals of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries that universal suffrage was achieved — women and non-propertied men organised opposition movements demanding equal political rights.

In the economic sphere, liberalism stood for the freedom of markets and the abolition of state-imposed restrictions on the movement of goods and capital. During the nineteenth century this was a strong demand of the emerging middle classes. A merchant named Friedrich List, a professor in Tübingen, wrote in 1834 about the German confederation: “the aim of the Zollverein is to bind the Germans economically into a nation… It aims at bringing the nation to a higher level of material prosperity by the free and unrestricted movement of goods.”

Such conditions were not achieved easily. In the first half of the nineteenth century, the German-speaking regions were divided into a large number of small states, each with its own currency, weights and measures. A merchant travelling in 1833 from Hamburg to Nuremberg to sell his goods had to pass through 11 customs barriers and pay a customs duty of about 5 per cent at each one; there were as many as thirty currencies and a bewildering variety of weights and measures. The Zollverein — a customs union formed in 1834 at the initiative of Prussia — abolished tariff barriers, reduced the number of currencies from over thirty to two, and created a network of railways that further stimulated mobility, harnessing economic interests to national unification.

Teacher explanation

A wave of economic nationalism strengthened wider nationalist sentiments. Economic liberalism and the unification of the German states went hand in hand.

A New Conservatism After 1815 — the Congress of Vienna

After Napoleon’s defeat, the victors met at the Congress of Vienna in 1815 to restore the monarchies overthrown by Napoleon and create a new conservative order in Europe. The conservative regimes were driven by a spirit of conservatism, which stressed the importance of tradition, established institutions and customs, and preferred gradual development to quick change.

The main intention was to restore the monarchies and create a new conservative order. The Congress of Vienna, hosted by the Austrian Chancellor Duke Metternich, was convened to restore stability and stability of Europe. Most of the delegates were conservatives and did not want the French Revolution to happen again.

The settlements of 1815 changed the map of Europe: the Bourbon dynasty, deposed during the French Revolution, was restored to power, and France lost the territories it had annexed under Napoleon. A series of states were set up on the boundaries of France to prevent French expansion in future: the kingdom of the Netherlands, which included Belgium, was set up in the north, and Genoa was added to Piedmont in the south. Prussia was given important new territories on its western frontiers, while Austria was given control of northern Italy. The German confederation of 39 states set up by Napoleon was left untouched. In the east, Russia was given part of Poland and Prussia was given a portion of Saxony.

The conservative order could not restore the abolition of serfdom and feudal privileges that had taken place during the Napoleonic wars, nor could it undo the administrative and legal reforms Napoleon had introduced. Above all, the memory of the French Revolution continued to inspire liberals — and the fear of revolution also shaped the policy of the rulers.

Sovereignty transferred from monarchy to citizens; la patrie, le citoyen, tricolour, uniform laws.
French armies carry nationalism into Holland, Belgium, Switzerland and much of Italy; Jacobin clubs spread.
Equality before law, right to property, abolition of birth privileges, simplified administration.
Conservative order restored; Metternich; buffer states created around France; German confederation of 39 states retained.
Bourbon kings overthrown; Belgium breaks away from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands.
Customs union at Prussia’s initiative; tariffs abolished, currencies reduced from over thirty to two.
Frankfurt Parliament meets in the Church of St Paul; liberal-nationalist demands.
William I proclaimed German Kaiser at Versailles; Victor Emmanuel II king of united Italy (1861).
The Revolution of 1830 and 1848 — the Frankfurt Parliament

The July Revolution of 1830 in France led to the overthrow of the Bourbon kings and the installation of a constitutional monarchy under Louis Philippe. The Belgian provinces broke away from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands and declared independence, and liberal-nationalists in many parts of Europe began to demand national unification.

The revolution of 1848 was the most widespread. Food shortages and widespread unemployment brought the population of Paris out on the roads, and a republic based on universal male suffrage was proclaimed. It was followed by upheavals in Austria, Germany and Italy: in 1848 the liberal-nationalists of Germany demanded the creation of a nation-state, and the Frankfurt Parliament met in the Church of St Paul on 18 May 1848. It was attended by 831 elected representatives, drawn largely from the middle classes — professionals, businessmen and property owners — who had drafted a constitution for a German nation to be headed by a monarchy subject to a parliament.

They offered the crown to Friedrich Wilhelm IV, King of Prussia, but he rejected it, saying he would not accept a crown “from the gutter”, and joined other monarchs to oppose the elected assembly. The parliament was dominated by the middle classes, who resisted the demands of workers and artisans and consequently lost their support. In the end, troops were called in and the assembly was forced to disband.

The political associations and clubs formed by women, and the many women who participated in the Frankfurt Parliament as observers, show that women had begun to claim a political role — Louise Otto-Peters founded a women’s journal and a political association in Germany. Yet when the Frankfurt Parliament assembled, women were denied the right to vote, and they were admitted only as observers to stand in the visitors’ gallery.

Source analysis

The Club of Thinkers: the anonymous caricature of The Club of Thinkers (c. 1819) shows men in a debating club — a satirical comment on the new political societies and on the exclusion of women from them. The cartoon asks you to notice who is inside the room and who is not.

The Unification of Germany

After 1848, nationalism in Europe moved away from its association with democracy and revolution. Nationalist sentiments were often mobilised by conservatives to promote state power and achieve political domination over Europe. This process of nation-building, though, was accompanied by great brutality: subject peoples were made to accept the new states and abandon their own traditions, languages and customs, and a large part of the Balkan region came under Ottoman rule.

Prussia took the leadership in the movement for national unification. Its chief minister, Otto von Bismarck, was the architect of this process, carried out with the help of the Prussian army and bureaucracy. Three wars over seven years — with Austria, Denmark and France — ended in Prussian victory and completed the process of unification. On 18 January 1871, in the Hall of Mirrors in the Palace of Versailles, the Prussian king, William I, was proclaimed German Emperor (Kaiser).

The new German state placed emphasis on modernising the currency, banking, legal and judicial systems. Prussian measures such as the abolition of serfdom, and the removal of restrictions on the movement of goods and capital, were extended to other parts of Germany.

Bismarck’s policy is summed up in his famous phrase “blood and iron” — the unification was achieved not by speeches and majority resolutions but by war. The Junkers, the large landowners of Prussia, dominated the united Germany’s army and bureaucracy, and the new state was a strong, authoritarian, militarised empire rather than a democratic one.

The Unification of Italy

Italy had a long history of political fragmentation. Italians were scattered over several dynastic states as well as the multi-national Habsburg Empire. During the middle of the nineteenth century, Italy was divided into seven states, of which only one, Sardinia-Piedmont, was ruled by an Italian princely house. The north was under Austrian Habsburgs, the centre was ruled by the Pope and the southern regions were under the domination of the Bourbon kings of Spain. Even the Italian language had not acquired one common form and still had many regional and local variations.

During the 1830s, Giuseppe Mazzini put together a coherent programme for a unitary Italian Republic and had formed a secret society called Young Italy in Marseille; he also founded Young Europe in Berne in 1833. He believed that God had intended nations to be the natural units of mankind, and his relentless opposition to monarchy and his vision of democratic republics frightened the conservatives. Metternich described him as “the most dangerous enemy of our social order”.

Following the failure of revolutionary uprisings in 1831 and 1848, the mantle of Italian unification fell on Sardinia-Piedmont and its king Victor Emmanuel II. Its chief minister, Count Camillo de Cavour, who was neither a revolutionary nor a democrat, led the movement to unify the regions of Italy through diplomacy and a tactful alliance with France, which helped defeat Austrian forces in 1859. Cavour was much more successful than Mazzini and the revolutionaries, and in 1860 the forces of the Kingdom of Sardinia-Piedmont moved into southern Italy and the kingdom of the Two Sicilies.

In 1860, Giuseppe Garibaldi and his Red Shirts marched into South Italy and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies and succeeded in winning the support of the local peasants in order to drive out the Spanish rulers. In 1861, Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed king of united Italy.

Much of the Italian population, among whom rates of illiteracy were very high, remained blissfully unaware of liberal-nationalist ideology. The peasant masses who had supported Garibaldi in southern Italy had never heard of Italia, and believed that “La Talia” was Victor Emmanuel’s wife! The cartoon of Garibaldi holding King Victor Emmanuel II of Sardinia-Piedmont to the “boot named Italy” captures both the achievement and its awkwardness.

The Strange Case of Britain

In Britain the formation of the nation-state was not the result of a sudden upheaval or revolution but of a long-drawn-out process. There was no British nation prior to the eighteenth century; the primary identities of the people who inhabited the British Isles were ethnic — English, Welsh, Scot or Irish — each with its own cultural and political traditions. As the English nation steadily grew in wealth, importance and power, it was able to extend its influence over the other nations of the islands.

The English parliament, which had seized power from the monarchy in 1688 after a prolonged conflict, was the instrument through which a nation-state, with England at its centre, came to be forged. The Act of Union between England and Scotland in 1707 resulted in the formation of the “United Kingdom of Great Britain” — in effect, a single British parliament dominated by England. In 1801 Ireland was forced to join the union, and a new “United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland” was formed.

A new British nation was forged through the propagation of a dominant English culture, helped by the growth of the British identity, the British flag (the Union Jack), the anthem (“God Save Our Noble King”) and the English language, which steadily became the language of the nation and actively suppressed the distinctive cultures and languages of the other nations.

The Scottish Highlands suffered a terrible repression whenever they attempted to assert their independence: the Catholic clans that inhabited the Scottish Highlands suffered terrible repression whenever they attempted to assert their independence, the Scottish Highlanders were forbidden to speak their Gaelic language or wear their national dress, and large numbers were forcibly driven out of their homeland. Ireland faced similar treatment: the English helped the Protestants of Ireland to establish dominance over a largely Catholic country, and the Irish Catholics revolted against British dominance, with Wolfe Tone and the United Irishmen leading a famous but failed revolt in 1798.

So the British nation-state was made by parliament, war and cultural domination, not by a revolutionary demand for popular sovereignty — which is why the chapter says the history of nationalism in Britain was unlike the rest of Europe.

Visualising the Nation — Allegory, Marianne and Germania

Artists in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries represented the nation as a female figure. Nations were then portrayed as female figures, and the female form did not stand for any particular woman in real life — rather it was an allegory of the nation. In other words, the female figure became an allegorical representation of the nation.

In France, the nation was personified by a female figure called Marianne, a popular Christian name, which underlined the idea of a people’s nation. Her characteristics were drawn from those of Liberty and the Republic — the red cap, the tricolour and the cockade. Statues of Marianne were erected in public squares to remind the public of the national symbol of unity and to persuade them to identify with it. Marianne images were marked on coins and stamps.

Similarly, Germania became the allegory of the German nation. In visual representations, Germania wears a crown of oak leaves, as the German oak stands for heroism. In Philip Veit’s Germania (1848), the figure holds a sword and wears the crown of oak leaves, standing for the nation’s readiness to fight. Julius Hübner’s “The Fallen Germania” (1850) shows the nation defeated and mourning, while the later image of Germania guarding the Rhine shows her as a sentinel of the nation’s frontier.

Nationalism and Imperialism — the Balkans

By the last quarter of the nineteenth century, nationalism no longer retained its idealistic liberal-democratic sentiment of the first half of the century, but became a narrow creed and was increasingly identified with the desire for territory and power. Nationalist groups became increasingly intolerant and wanted to extend their influence over other nations.

The major European powers manipulated the nationalist aspirations of the subject peoples in Europe to further their own imperialist aims. The most serious source of nationalist tension in Europe after 1871 was the area called the Balkans. The Balkans was a region of geographical and ethnic variation comprising modern-day Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia and Montenegro, whose inhabitants were broadly known as the Slavs. A large part of the Balkans was under the control of the Ottoman Empire. The spread of the ideas of romantic nationalism in the Balkans together with the disintegration of the Ottoman Empire made this region very explosive.

The Balkan peoples based their claims for independence or political rights on nationality, and used history to prove that they had once been independent but had subsequently been subjugated by foreign powers. Hence the rebellious nationalities in the Balkans thought of their struggles as attempts to win back their long-lost independence. As the different Slavic nationalities struggled to define their identity and independence, the Balkan area became an area of intense conflict.

The Balkan states were fiercely jealous of each other and each hoped to gain more territory at the expense of the others. Matters were further complicated because the Balkans also became the scene of big power rivalry. During this period, there was intense rivalry among the European powers over trade and colonies as well as naval and military might, and each of these big powers was keen on countering the hold of other powers over the Balkans and extending its own control over the area. This led to a series of wars in the region and finally the First World War.

Nationalism, aligned with imperialism, led Europe to disaster in 1914. But meanwhile, many countries in the world which had been colonised by the European powers in the nineteenth century began to oppose imperial domination. The anti-imperial movements that developed everywhere were nationalist, in the sense that they all struggled to form independent nation-states and were inspired by a sense of collective national unity forged in confrontation with imperialism. European ideas of nationalism were nowhere replicated, for people everywhere developed their own specific variety of nationalism. But the idea that societies should be organised into “nation-states” came to be accepted as natural and universal.

The timeline at a glance

1789French Revolution — la patrie, le citoyen, tricolour, National Assembly

How to read this timeline: follow the two tracks — the revolutionary-liberal track (1789, 1830, 1848) and the state-building track (1815, 1834, 1861, 1871). The chapter’s argument is that nationalism moved from the first to the second, and then to imperialism.

07

NCERT In-text Questions and Answers

The questions printed inside the chapter

These are the “Can you…” and activity questions that appear inside the chapter text. Model answers are based on the chapter itself.

1.

What did Frédéric Sorrieu visualise in his prints?

Model answer

A world made up of “democratic and social Republics”. The peoples of Europe and America march in a long train past the Statue of Liberty, offering homage; on the earth lie the shattered remains of absolutist institutions; the peoples are grouped as distinct nations identified by flags and national costume, with the United States and Switzerland leading, then France with the tricolour, then Germany with a black-red-gold flag, then Austria, Poland and Hungary.

2.

What steps did French revolutionaries take to create a sense of collective identity?

Model answer

They introduced the ideas of la patrie and le citoyen to emphasise a united community of equal rights; chose the tricolour to replace the royal standard; elected the Estates General as the National Assembly; composed hymns, took oaths and commemorated martyrs in the name of the nation; set up a centralised administration with uniform laws; abolished internal customs duties and adopted uniform weights and measures; and discouraged regional dialects so that French, as spoken and written in Paris, became the common language of the nation.

3.

What did Napoleon do to make the administrative system more efficient?

Model answer

The Civil Code of 1804 (the Napoleonic Code) did away with privileges based on birth, established equality before the law and secured the right to property. He simplified administrative divisions, abolished the feudal system and freed peasants from serfdom and manorial dues; in towns guild restrictions were removed and transport and communication improved; and uniform laws, standardised weights and measures and a common national currency facilitated the movement of goods and capital. But these arrangements did not bring political freedom: increased taxation, censorship and forced conscription outweighed the advantages for many.

4.

What is meant by the 1848 revolution of the liberals? What political, social and economic ideas did the liberals support?

Model answer

It refers to the wave of revolutions in 1848 led by the educated liberal middle classes, who demanded the creation of nation-states on liberal principles — constitutions, parliaments, freedom of the press and association. Politically they wanted government by consent, equality before the law and, increasingly, universal male suffrage; socially they wanted an end to aristocratic privilege and, for some, the emancipation of women and the abolition of serfdom; economically they wanted freedom of markets, the abolition of state-imposed restrictions on the movement of goods and capital, uniform currency, weights and measures, and the removal of tariff barriers — which is what the Zollverein achieved.

5.

Choose three examples to show the contribution of culture to the growth of nationalism in Europe.

Model answer

(i) Romanticism — Herder and others held that true German culture was to be discovered among the common people, in folk songs, poetry and dances, which helped create a sense of a shared national culture. (ii) Language and print — the standardisation of a national language, as with French as spoken in Paris, and later print culture, made a common identity possible. (iii) Allegory and art — Marianne and Germania, the Statue of Liberty, flags, anthems, coins and stamps gave the nation a visible, shareable image. (Music, as in Poland, played a similar role.)

6.

Who were Marianne and Germania? What was the importance of the way in which they were portrayed?

Model answer

Marianne was the female allegory of the French nation — a popular Christian name that underlined the idea of a people’s nation — shown with the red cap, tricolour and cockade, and placed in statues, coins and stamps to remind the public of national unity. Germania was the allegory of the German nation, shown with a crown of oak leaves (heroism), a sword, an olive branch, the black-red-gold flag of the liberal-nationalists and rays of the rising sun. Their importance lies in allegory itself: because the nation is abstract, a female figure with recognisable attributes let ordinary people see it, identify with it, and accept it as natural — which is why the attributes carried meanings (readiness to fight, willingness to make peace, heroism, a new era).

7.

Briefly trace the process of German unification.

Model answer

After the failure of the 1848 Frankfurt Parliament, Prussia took the leadership. Its chief minister, Otto von Bismarck, carried out unification with the help of the Prussian army and bureaucracy through three wars over seven years — with Austria, Denmark and France — all of which Prussia won. On 18 January 1871, in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, the Prussian king William I was proclaimed German Emperor. The new state modernised the currency, banking and legal systems, and Prussian measures such as the abolition of serfdom and the removal of restrictions on the movement of goods and capital were extended to the rest of Germany. It was a strong, authoritarian state, its army and bureaucracy dominated by the Junkers.

8.

How was the history of nationalism in Britain unlike the rest of Europe?

Model answer

There was no British nation before the eighteenth century; the primary identities were ethnic — English, Welsh, Scot, Irish. The nation-state was formed not by revolution but by a long-drawn-out process: the English parliament seized power from the monarchy in 1688, the Act of Union with Scotland in 1707 created the United Kingdom of Great Britain, and Ireland was forcibly joined in 1801. British identity was forged through a dominant English culture, the Union Jack, the anthem and the English language — and through repression, as with the Scottish Highlands, where Gaelic and the national dress were banned, and Ireland, where Protestants were helped to dominate a Catholic country and Wolfe Tone’s revolt of 1798 was crushed.

9.

Why did nationalist tensions emerge in the Balkans?

Model answer

Because the Balkans was a region of great geographical and ethnic variety — modern Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia and Montenegro — whose inhabitants, broadly the Slavs, were largely under the Ottoman Empire. The spread of romantic nationalism together with the disintegration of the Ottoman Empire made the region explosive. The Balkan peoples based their claims on nationality and used history to prove that they had once been independent, so each nationality saw its struggle as recovering a long-lost independence. The states were fiercely jealous of one another and each hoped to gain territory at the others’ expense, while the big European powers competed for influence over the region — producing a series of wars and finally the First World War.

10.

What did the Greek war of independence contribute to the idea of nationalism?

Model answer

Greece had been part of the Ottoman Empire since the fifteenth century. The growth of revolutionary nationalism in Europe sparked a struggle for independence among the Greeks in 1821, and nationalists in Greece were supported by other Greeks living in exile and by many West Europeans who had sympathies for ancient Greek culture. Poets and artists mobilised public opinion, as Delacroix did with “The Massacre at Chios” (1824), and the Treaty of Constantinople of 1832 recognised Greece as an independent nation. It showed that culture — poetry, art, sympathy for a classical past — could mobilise a nation and its European supporters.

11.

What was the role of women in nationalist struggles?

Model answer

Women participated in nationalist struggles as organisers, writers and campaigners, and formed political associations and journals — Louise Otto-Peters founded a women’s journal and a political association in Germany. Yet they were denied political rights: in the Frankfurt Parliament, women were admitted only as observers to stand in the visitors’ gallery, and they had no vote. The chapter notes that women and non-propertied men had to organise opposition movements over the nineteenth and twentieth centuries to win equal political rights.

08

NCERT Exercise Questions and Answers

End-of-chapter exercises, projects and activities

NCERT Exercises

Reproduced from the exercise section of the chapter, with model answers. Word limits are the ones the textbook sets.

1.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Write a note on: (a) Giuseppe Mazzini (b) Count Camillo de Cavour (c) The Greek war of independence (d) Frankfurt parliament (e) The role of women in nationalist struggles.

Model answer

(a) Mazzini: born in Genoa in 1807, he founded two secret societies — Young Italy in Marseille and Young Europe in Berne (1833) — and put together a coherent programme for a unitary Italian Republic, believing that God had intended nations to be the natural units of mankind. Metternich called him “the most dangerous enemy of our social order”. (b) Cavour: Chief Minister of Sardinia-Piedmont, neither a revolutionary nor a democrat; he led unification through diplomacy and a tactful alliance with France, which helped defeat Austrian forces in 1859, and was more successful than Mazzini and the revolutionaries. (c) Greek war of independence: Greece had been part of the Ottoman Empire since the fifteenth century; revolutionary nationalism sparked a struggle in 1821, supported by Greeks in exile and by West Europeans sympathetic to ancient Greek culture, with poets and artists mobilising opinion; the Treaty of Constantinople in 1832 recognised Greece as an independent nation. (d) Frankfurt Parliament: convened in the Church of St Paul on 18 May 1848, with 831 elected representatives, largely middle class; it drafted a constitution for a German nation headed by a monarchy subject to a parliament, and offered the crown to Friedrich Wilhelm IV of Prussia, who rejected it; dominated by the middle classes, it lost workers’ support, and troops disbanded it. (e) Women: they participated in associations, journals and campaigns — Louise Otto-Peters founded a women’s journal and political association — but were denied the vote and admitted to the Frankfurt Parliament only as observers in the visitors’ gallery.

2.
NCERT exercise3 marks

What steps did the French revolutionaries take to create a sense of collective identity among the French people?

Model answer

The ideas of la patrie and le citoyen; the tricolour replacing the royal standard; the Estates General renamed the National Assembly; hymns, oaths and the commemoration of martyrs; a centralised administration with uniform laws; the abolition of internal customs duties and adoption of uniform weights and measures; and the discouragement of regional dialects so that French became the common language of the nation.

3.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Who were Marianne and Germania? What was the importance of the way in which they were portrayed?

Model answer

They were the female allegories of the French and German nations. Marianne carried the red cap, tricolour and cockade and appeared on coins, stamps and statues; Germania wore a crown of oak leaves and held a sword with an olive branch, with the black-red-gold flag and rays of the rising sun. Portraying the nation as a woman with recognisable attributes made an abstract idea visible and lovable: people could identify with the figure and accept the nation as natural, and each attribute — heroism, readiness to fight, willingness to make peace, a new era — carried a political message.

4.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Briefly trace the process of German unification.

Model answer

After 1848 Prussia led the movement. Bismarck, its chief minister, used the army and bureaucracy in three wars over seven years — against Austria, Denmark and France — all of which Prussia won. On 18 January 1871 William I was proclaimed German Emperor at Versailles. The new state modernised currency, banking and the legal system, and extended Prussian reforms such as the abolition of serfdom to other parts of Germany. It was authoritarian and militarised, dominated by the Junkers.

5.
NCERT exercise3 marks

What changes did Napoleon introduce to make the administrative system more efficient in the territories ruled by him?

Model answer

The Civil Code of 1804 abolished privileges based on birth, established equality before the law and secured the right to property; administrative divisions were simplified; the feudal system was abolished and peasants freed from serfdom and manorial dues; guild restrictions were removed in towns; transport and communication were improved; and uniform laws, standardised weights and measures and a common currency facilitated trade. But political freedom did not follow: taxation, censorship and conscription caused resentment.

6.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Explain what is meant by the 1848 revolution of the liberals. What were the political, social and economic ideas supported by the liberals?

Model answer

It was the wave of revolutions led by the educated liberal middle classes demanding nation-states on liberal principles. Politically: government by consent, equality before the law, constitutions and parliaments, freedom of the press and association, and eventually universal suffrage. Socially: an end to privileges based on birth, and demands for women’s rights and the abolition of serfdom. Economically: freedom of markets, abolition of state-imposed restrictions on goods and capital, uniform currency and weights and measures, and the removal of tariff barriers — as achieved by the Zollverein.

7.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Choose three examples to show the contribution of culture to the growth of nationalism in Europe.

Model answer

Romanticism — the celebration of folk culture, songs and poetry as the true expression of the nation; language — the standardisation of a national language and its use in print, which made a shared identity possible; and allegory and art — Marianne, Germania, flags, anthems, coins and stamps, which gave the nation a visible and shareable image. Music and painting, as in Poland and Greece, played the same role.

8.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Through a focus on any two countries, explain how nations developed over the nineteenth century.

Model answer

Germany: from a confederation of 39 states, economic unity came first through the Zollverein of 1834; the 1848 Frankfurt Parliament failed when the king refused the crown; Prussia then unified the country through Bismarck’s three wars, and the empire was proclaimed at Versailles in 1871. Italy: divided into seven states, it was unified through Mazzini’s secret societies and republican programme, Cavour’s diplomacy and alliance with France in 1859, and Garibaldi’s Red Shirts in the south in 1860, with Victor Emmanuel II proclaimed king in 1861. In both cases war, diplomacy and popular mobilisation worked together.

9.
NCERT exercise3 marks

How was the history of nationalism in Britain unlike the rest of Europe?

Model answer

Because it was not produced by revolution but by a long process of parliamentary and military consolidation: the English parliament seized power in 1688, the Act of Union with Scotland in 1707 created Great Britain, and Ireland was forcibly joined in 1801. British identity was propagated through a dominant English culture — the Union Jack, the anthem and the English language — and through the repression of other cultures, as in the Scottish Highlands and Ireland.

10.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Why did nationalist tensions emerge in the Balkans?

Model answer

Because the region’s ethnic variety and the disintegration of Ottoman rule, combined with the spread of romantic nationalism, made it explosive. The Balkan peoples claimed independence on the basis of nationality and history, the states were jealous of one another and sought territory at each other’s expense, and the great powers competed for influence there — leading to a series of wars and finally the First World War.

11.
NCERT projectProject

Project — find out more about nationalist symbols in countries outside Europe. For one or two countries, collect examples of pictures, posters or music that are symbols of nationalism. How are these different from European examples?

Model answer

For example, India’s national flag, the Ashoka emblem, “Vande Mataram” and “Jana Gana Mana”; or Ireland’s harp and shamrock. Differences worth noting: anti-colonial nationalism often used symbols of an indigenous past or of religious and folk tradition rather than classical allegory, and its female figures (Bharat Mata, for instance) were drawn from religious and rural imagery rather than from Greco-Roman Liberty. 09

Important Questions and Answers

Board-style practice

Practice questions

Written in the style of CBSE board papers. They are additional practice, not NCERT originals.

1.

What is a nation-state? How did the French Revolution create one? (5 marks)

Model answer

A nation-state is a state in which the majority of citizens, and not only its rulers, develop a sense of common identity and shared history or descent — a commonness forged through struggles and the actions of leaders and ordinary people. The French Revolution of 1789 transferred sovereignty from the monarchy to a body of citizens and proclaimed that the people would constitute the nation. It created collective identity through la patrie and le citoyen, the tricolour, the National Assembly, hymns, oaths and martyrs’ commemorations, a centralised administration with uniform laws, the abolition of internal customs and adoption of uniform weights and measures, and the promotion of French as the common language. It also declared it the mission of the French nation to liberate the peoples of Europe from despotism, and French armies carried these ideas abroad in the 1790s.

2.

Explain the role of liberalism in the making of nationalism. (5 marks)

Model answer

Liberalism, from the Latin liber (free), stood for freedom for the individual and equality of all before the law. Politically it meant government by consent, and it inspired the revolutionaries in France — though in revolutionary France the vote was limited to property-owning men, and women and the propertyless had to struggle for decades for equal political rights. Economically, liberalism stood for the freedom of markets and the abolition of state-imposed restrictions on the movement of goods and capital. In the German-speaking regions, where a merchant crossing from Hamburg to Nuremberg in 1833 passed eleven customs barriers, paid about 5 per cent at each and faced thirty currencies, this demand produced the Zollverein of 1834 — a customs union at Prussia’s initiative that abolished tariffs, cut currencies from over thirty to two and built railways, harnessing economic interests to national unification.

3.

Describe the conservative order established at Vienna in 1815, and explain why it could not last. (5 marks)

Model answer

After Napoleon’s defeat the victors met at the Congress of Vienna in 1815, hosted by Metternich, to restore the monarchies and create a conservative order based on tradition and gradual change. The Bourbon dynasty was restored in France, which lost the territories annexed under Napoleon; buffer states were created — the kingdom of the Netherlands including Belgium in the north, Genoa added to Piedmont in the south; Prussia gained territories on its western frontiers and part of Saxony; Austria was given control of northern Italy; Russia got part of Poland; and the German confederation of 39 states was left untouched. It could not last because the conservative order could not undo the abolition of serfdom and feudal privileges or the administrative and legal reforms of the Napoleonic period, and above all because the memory of the French Revolution continued to inspire liberals — producing the revolutions of 1830 and 1848.

4.

Explain the unification of Italy. (5 marks)

Model answer

Italy was divided into seven states, only one of which — Sardinia-Piedmont — was ruled by an Italian princely house; the north was under the Habsburgs, the centre under the Pope and the south under the Bourbon kings of Spain, and even the language had many regional variations. Mazzini founded Young Italy in Marseille and Young Europe in Berne (1833) and put forward a programme for a unitary Italian Republic, but the revolutionary uprisings of 1831 and 1848 failed. The leadership then passed to Sardinia-Piedmont and Victor Emmanuel II, whose chief minister Cavour — neither a revolutionary nor a democrat — unified the regions through diplomacy and an alliance with France that helped defeat Austria in 1859. In 1860 Garibaldi and his Red Shirts marched into southern Italy and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, winning peasant support against the Spanish rulers, and in 1861 Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed king of united Italy. Yet most of the illiterate peasantry remained unaware of liberal-nationalist ideology — some believed “La Talia” was the king’s wife.

5.

How did Britain become a nation-state, and how was its path different? (5 marks)

Model answer

There was no British nation before the eighteenth century; identities were ethnic — English, Welsh, Scot, Irish. As the English nation grew in wealth and power it extended its influence over the islands. The English parliament, which had seized power from the monarchy in 1688, was the instrument: the Act of Union with Scotland in 1707 formed the United Kingdom of Great Britain with a single parliament dominated by England, and Ireland was forcibly joined in 1801. A British identity was propagated through a dominant English culture — the Union Jack, “God Save Our Noble King” and the English language — and through repression: Catholic clans of the Scottish Highlands were forbidden to speak Gaelic or wear their national dress and many were driven from their homeland, while in Ireland Protestants were helped to dominate a largely Catholic country and Wolfe Tone’s United Irishmen revolt of 1798 was crushed. The path was therefore evolutionary and parliamentary, not revolutionary, and it was built on cultural domination rather than popular sovereignty.

6.

Explain the significance of the allegorical figures Marianne and Germania, and the attributes used with them. (5 marks)

Model answer

Because the nation is abstract, artists represented it as a female figure — an allegory. Marianne personified France, her name a popular Christian name underlining the idea of a people’s nation, with the red cap, tricolour and cockade; her statues in public squares reminded people of national unity, and her image appeared on coins and stamps. Germania personified Germany with a crown of oak leaves (heroism), a breastplate with an eagle (the German empire’s strength), a sword (readiness to fight) with an olive branch (willingness to make peace), the black-red-gold tricolour of the liberal-nationalists of 1848 (banned by the German dukes) and rays of the rising sun (a new era). Philip Veit’s Germania of 1848, Julius Hübner’s “The Fallen Germania” of 1850 and the later Germania guarding the Rhine show how the same figure could express triumph, mourning and defence.

7.

How did nationalism turn into imperialism, and what was the result? (5 marks)

Model answer

By the last quarter of the nineteenth century nationalism lost its liberal-democratic idealism and became a narrow creed identified with the desire for territory and power; nationalist groups became intolerant and wanted to extend their influence over other nations, and the European powers manipulated subject peoples’ nationalism for imperial ends. The most serious source of tension after 1871 was the Balkans — a region of great ethnic variety whose inhabitants, broadly Slavs, were largely under the Ottoman Empire. Romantic nationalism and the disintegration of Ottoman rule made the region explosive: Balkan peoples claimed independence on the basis of nationality and history, the states were jealous of one another and each hoped to gain territory at the others’ expense, and the great powers competed for influence. This produced a series of wars and finally the First World War in 1914. Meanwhile colonised peoples turned nationalism against their imperial rulers, and the idea of the nation-state became accepted as natural and universal.

8.

Why did the Frankfurt Parliament fail? (3 marks)

Model answer

Because the King of Prussia, Friedrich Wilhelm IV, rejected the crown offered by the Assembly, saying he would not accept a crown “from the gutter”, and joined other monarchs in opposing the elected assembly; and because the parliament was dominated by the middle classes, who resisted the demands of workers and artisans and thereby lost their support. In the end troops were called in and the assembly was forced to disband.

9.

What was the Zollverein and why was it important? (3 marks)

Model answer

It was a customs union formed in 1834 at the initiative of Prussia. It abolished tariff barriers, reduced the number of currencies from over thirty to two and created a network of railways that stimulated mobility. It is important because it harnessed economic interests to national unification — economic liberalism and the unification of the German states went hand in hand.

Frequently Asked Questions

Quick clarifications

1.

What is the difference between a nation and a nation-state?

Model answer

A nation is a community with a sense of shared identity, history and descent; a nation-state is a state whose citizens — not only its rulers — share that identity, with a constitution, territory and sovereignty.

2.

Was Napoleon a nationalist?

Model answer

He spread some revolutionary principles administratively — equality before the law, the abolition of feudalism, uniform laws — but he also destroyed democracy in France and imposed conscription and censorship abroad. The chapter presents him as an administrator who carried some nationalist ideas while ruling as a monarch.

3.

Why did the 1848 revolutions fail?

Model answer

Because the monarchs refused to concede — Friedrich Wilhelm IV rejected the crown — and because the liberal middle classes in the Frankfurt Parliament resisted workers’ and artisans’ demands, losing popular support, after which troops disbanded the assembly.

4.

Who were the Junkers?

Model answer

The large landowners of Prussia, who dominated the army and bureaucracy of the new German empire.

5.

What is meant by “blood and iron”?

Model answer

Bismarck’s description of his method — unification achieved by war and state power rather than by speeches and majority resolutions.

6.

Why is Sorrieu’s vision called utopian?

Model answer

Because a world of peacefully coexisting democratic republics was an ideal that did not exist and was unlikely to — Europe was in the middle of revolutions and wars.

7.

Did women participate in nationalist struggles?

Model answer

Yes — in associations, journals and campaigns, as Louise Otto-Peters did in Germany — but they were denied the vote and admitted to the Frankfurt Parliament only as observers.

8.

What did the Treaty of Constantinople do?

Model answer

It recognised Greece as an independent nation in 1832, after the Greek struggle for independence that began in 1821.

12

Assertion-Reason Questions

Choose the correct option

How to answer

(a) Both A and R are true and R explains A. (b) Both are true but R does not explain A. (c) A is true, R is false. (d) A is false, R is true.

1.

Assertion (A): The French Revolution produced the first clear expression of nationalism.
Reason (R): It transferred sovereignty from the monarchy to a body of French citizens.

2.

Assertion (A): The Napoleonic Code established equality before the law.
Reason (R): It also gave the French people political freedom.

3.

Assertion (A): The Zollverein strengthened economic nationalism in Germany.
Reason (R): It abolished tariff barriers and reduced the number of currencies from over thirty to two.

4.

Assertion (A): The Congress of Vienna restored the conservative order in Europe.
Reason (R): It was hosted by Duke Metternich.

5.

Assertion (A): The Frankfurt Parliament succeeded in creating a German nation-state.
Reason (R): Friedrich Wilhelm IV rejected the crown offered by the Assembly.

6.

Assertion (A): Germany was unified through war and diplomacy.
Reason (R): Bismarck fought three wars over seven years with Austria, Denmark and France.

7.

Assertion (A): Garibaldi’s Red Shirts won the support of peasants in southern Italy.
Reason (R): They were driving out the Spanish Bourbon rulers.

8.

Assertion (A): The British nation-state was formed by a sudden revolution.
Reason (R): It was the result of a long-drawn-out process.

9.

Assertion (A): Marianne and Germania were allegories of their nations.
Reason (R): They were portraits of real women who led nationalist movements.

10.

Assertion (A): Nationalism in the Balkans contributed to the First World War.
Reason (R): The Balkan states were jealous of each other and the great powers competed for influence there.

Source-Based and Case-Based Questions

Read the passage or table, then answer

Source 1 — Ernst Renan, “What is a Nation?” (1882)

Source extract

“A nation is the culmination of a long past of endeavours, sacrifice and devotion. A heroic past, great men, glory, that is the social capital upon which one bases a national idea. To have common glories in the past, to have a common will in the present, to have performed great deeds together, to wish to perform still more — these are the essential conditions of being a people. A nation is therefore a large-scale solidarity… Its existence is a daily plebiscite… A province is its inhabitants; if anyone has the right to be consulted, it is the inhabitant. A nation never has any real interest in annexing or holding on to a country against its will. The existence of nations is a good thing, a necessity even. Their existence is a guarantee of liberty, which would be lost if the world had only one law and only one master.”

1.

What does Renan mean by calling a nation “a daily plebiscite”?

Model answer

That a nation is not a fixed, inherited thing but is re-created every day by the consent of its members — a continuous, daily agreement to live together, not a single act of founding.

2.

What are the “essential conditions of being a people” according to Renan?

Model answer

Common glories in the past, a common will in the present, having performed great deeds together, and the wish to perform still more — a large-scale solidarity built on shared memory and shared intention.

3.

Why does Renan say nations guarantee liberty?

Model answer

Because a world with “only one law and only one master” would be a world without liberty; the existence of separate nations prevents a single universal despotism. It is an argument against empire, and it explains why the idea of the nation-state spread.

Source 2 — The Zollverein and economic nationalism

Source extract

In the first half of the nineteenth century, the German-speaking regions were divided into a large number of small states, each with its own currency, weights and measures. A merchant travelling in 1833 from Hamburg to Nuremberg to sell his goods had to pass through 11 customs barriers and pay a customs duty of about 5 per cent at each one. There were as many as thirty currencies and a bewildering variety of weights and measures. The Zollverein — a customs union formed in 1834 at the initiative of Prussia — abolished tariff barriers, reduced the number of currencies from over thirty to two, and created a network of railways that further stimulated mobility, harnessing economic interests to national unification.

1.

What did the merchant’s journey show?

Model answer

That the fragmentation of Germany into many small states imposed real costs on trade: eleven customs barriers, about 5 per cent duty at each, and thirty currencies — a direct economic argument for unification.

2.

How did the Zollverein change this?

Model answer

It abolished tariff barriers, cut currencies from over thirty to two, and built railways that increased mobility, so goods and capital could move freely within a large market.

3.

What is the chapter’s larger point?

Model answer

That economic interests can be harnessed to national unification — economic liberalism and the making of the German nation went hand in hand, which is why the middle classes became the carriers of nationalist sentiment.

Source 3 — The making of British identity

Source extract

The English parliament, which had seized power from the monarchy in 1688 after a prolonged conflict, was the instrument through which a nation-state, with England at its centre, came to be forged. The Act of Union between England and Scotland in 1707 resulted in the formation of the “United Kingdom of Great Britain” — in effect, a single British parliament dominated by England. In 1801 Ireland was forced to join the union… The Scottish Highlands suffered a terrible repression whenever they attempted to assert their independence: the Scottish Highlanders were forbidden to speak their Gaelic language or wear their national dress, and large numbers were forcibly driven out of their homeland.

1.

What instrument forged the British nation-state?

Model answer

The English parliament, which had seized power from the monarchy in 1688, together with the Acts of Union — with Scotland in 1707 and with Ireland in 1801.

2.

What does the treatment of the Highlands show?

Model answer

That British identity was built on a dominant English culture and on repression: the Gaelic language and national dress were banned and Highlanders were driven from their land. Nation-building was not a peaceful, consensual process.

3.

How does this compare with France?

Model answer

France made the nation through a revolution that proclaimed popular sovereignty; Britain made it through parliamentary consolidation, war and cultural domination. That is why the chapter says the history of nationalism in Britain was unlike the rest of Europe.

Map-Based Practice

Locate and label on the outline map

How to practise

Read the task, then say or write the location before revealing the answer. Where a textbook map is available it is shown above with hotspots you can tap.

Map work — Europe after Vienna and the unifications

The map above is the original NCERT map — tap it to zoom. Then tap a numbered label below to check what to locate and where it lies.

1.

On an outline map of Europe, mark the states created or changed by the Congress of Vienna in 1815.

Model answer

France (Bourbons restored), the kingdom of the Netherlands including Belgium, Piedmont with Genoa, Prussia with new western territories and part of Saxony, Austria with northern Italy, Russia with part of Poland, and the German confederation of 39 states.

2.

Mark the seven states of Italy before unification and the areas added by 1861.

Model answer

Before 1861: Sardinia-Piedmont, Lombardy, Venetia, Parma, Modena, Tuscany, the Papal States and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies (often counted as seven principal states). By 1861 most of these, including the south won by Garibaldi, were joined to the kingdom of Italy under Victor Emmanuel II; Venetia (1866) and Rome (1870) followed later.

3.

Using the map of German unification, name the territories Prussia gained in 1866 and 1871.

Model answer

In 1866, after the war with Austria, Prussia annexed Schleswig-Holstein, Hanover, Hesse-Kassel, Nassau and Frankfurt; in 1871, after the war with France, it gained Alsace and Lorraine, and the southern German states joined the empire.

4.

Locate the Balkan region and name the modern countries that made it up.

Model answer

Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia and Montenegro — a region of great geographical and ethnic variation, largely under the Ottoman Empire, and the most serious source of tension in Europe after 1871.

HOTS and Competency-Based Questions

Think beyond the text

Higher order thinking

These ask you to apply, compare or evaluate. Model answers are indicative — your own well-reasoned answer can differ.

1.

“The nation is imagined before it is built.” Discuss with Sorrieu, Renan and the allegories.

Model answer

Yes — and that is the chapter’s method. Sorrieu imagined a world of democratic republics before it existed; Renan argued that a nation is a “daily plebiscite”, a shared will rather than a physical fact; and Marianne and Germania gave the nation a body and a face so that people could imagine belonging to it. Only after this imaginative work could Bismarck’s wars and Cavour’s diplomacy build actual states. Imagination is not decoration in nationalism; it is the raw material. (Model answer.)

2.

Was German unification a triumph of nationalism or of Prussian power?

Model answer

Both, in sequence. The demand for a nation came from liberals and the middle classes — the Zollverein, the 1848 parliament — but that route failed when the king refused the crown. Unification was then achieved by Prussian state power: Bismarck’s army, bureaucracy and three wars, with a Kaiser proclaimed at Versailles and the Junkers dominating the new state. So nationalism supplied the goal and the legitimacy; Prussia supplied the means and took the power. The result was a nation-state that was strong but not democratic. (Model answer.)

3.

Why did the same idea — nationalism — produce liberal democracy in France and authoritarian empire in Germany?

Model answer

Because the social forces carrying it differed. In France the revolution mobilised peasants and the urban population against a monarchy and aristocracy, and sovereignty passed to the citizens. In Germany the liberal middle class was weaker and divided, the 1848 parliament had no power to enforce its constitution, and unification was carried out by an existing monarchy and its army, which kept authority in the crown, the bureaucracy and the Junkers. Nationalism is a goal, not a form of government; the form depends on who leads. (Model answer.)

4.

How does the treatment of Scotland and Ireland complicate the story of British nation-building?

Model answer

It shows that a nation-state can be built by domination as well as by consent. British identity was propagated through a dominant English culture — the Union Jack, the anthem, the English language — while Gaelic was banned, Highland dress forbidden and Highlanders driven off their land, and Ireland was forcibly joined and its Catholic majority ruled by a Protestant minority. So the “United Kingdom” was unified in law but not in sentiment, which is why Irish nationalism remained a live force into the twentieth century. (Model answer.)

5.

What does the Balkans tell us about the dangers of nationalism?

Model answer

That nationalism without a framework for accommodation becomes competitive and then violent. In the Balkans each nationality claimed independence on the basis of history and ethnicity, each state wanted territory at its neighbour’s expense, and the great powers manipulated these claims for imperial advantage — producing a series of wars and finally the First World War. The lesson the chapter draws is that nationalism aligned with imperialism led Europe to disaster in 1914. (Model answer.)

6.

Were the 1848 revolutions a failure?

Model answer

In the short term, yes: the Frankfurt Parliament was disbanded, the king refused the crown, and monarchs regained control. In the longer term, no: 1848 put liberal and national demands on the European agenda, produced the vocabulary of constitutions, parliaments and universal male suffrage, and created the political organisations — including women’s associations — that later movements built on. Within twenty-three years both Germany and Italy were unified, which was the 1848 programme realised by other means. (Model answer.)

Quick Revision Sheet

One page before the exam

Sorrieu

  • 1848 prints of “democratic and social republics”; peoples march past the Statue of Liberty.
  • Shattered symbols of absolutism on the ground; nations identified by flags and costume.

France

  • 1789: sovereignty from monarchy to citizens; la patrie, le citoyen, tricolour, National Assembly.
  • Hymns, oaths, martyrs; uniform laws, weights and measures; French as common language.
  • Napoleon: Civil Code 1804 — equality before law, right to property, end of feudalism; but no political freedom.

Renan

  • 1882 Sorbonne lecture: a nation is “a daily plebiscite”, a large-scale solidarity.
  • Nations guarantee liberty against “one law and one master”.

Liberalism

  • From liber = free: individual freedom, equality before law, government by consent.
  • Economically: free markets. Zollverein 1834 — tariffs abolished, currencies 30+ → 2, railways.

Vienna 1815

  • Metternich; Bourbons restored; buffer states (Netherlands + Belgium, Genoa + Piedmont).
  • Austria gets northern Italy; Prussia gets western territories and part of Saxony; German confederation of 39 states; Russia gets part of Poland.

1830 and 1848

  • 1830: July Revolution in France; Belgium independent.
  • 1848: food shortages and unemployment; republic with universal male suffrage.
  • Frankfurt Parliament, 18 May 1848, Church of St Paul, 831 members; crown refused by Friedrich Wilhelm IV; disbanded by troops.
  • Women: associations and journals (Louise Otto-Peters) but no vote — observers only.

Germany

  • Prussia leads; Bismarck; three wars in seven years (Austria, Denmark, France).
  • 18 Jan 1871: William I proclaimed Kaiser at Versailles.
  • Modern currency, banking, legal system; Junkers dominate army and bureaucracy.

Italy

  • Seven states; Mazzini — Young Italy (Marseille), Young Europe (Berne 1833).
  • Cavour — diplomacy and alliance with France, 1859.
  • Garibaldi — Red Shirts, south, 1860; Victor Emmanuel II king, 1861.

Britain

  • 1688 parliament seizes power; 1707 Act of Union with Scotland; 1801 Ireland.
  • Union Jack, anthem, English language; Gaelic and Highland dress banned; 1798 Wolfe Tone revolt crushed.

Allegory

  • Marianne: red cap, tricolour, cockade; coins, stamps, statues.
  • Germania: oak crown (heroism), sword, olive branch, black-red-gold flag, rising sun.

Balkans

  • After 1871 the flashpoint; Ottoman disintegration + romantic nationalism.
  • Jealous states, great-power rivalry → wars → First World War 1914.
  • Anti-imperial nationalism elsewhere; nation-state becomes universal idea.

Chapter Summary

The whole chapter in a few paragraphs

In 1848 Frédéric Sorrieu imagined a world of “democratic and social republics”, with the peoples of Europe and America marching past the Statue of Liberty and the shattered symbols of absolutism underfoot. The first clear expression of nationalism came from the French Revolution of 1789, which transferred sovereignty from the monarchy to the citizens and created a collective identity through la patrie and le citoyen, the tricolour, the National Assembly, hymns, oaths and martyrs, uniform laws, weights and measures, and a common language. Napoleon spread some of these principles through the Civil Code of 1804 — equality before the law, the right to property, the abolition of feudalism — but without political freedom. Ernst Renan later defined a nation as “a daily plebiscite”, a large-scale solidarity of shared memory and present will.

Liberalism, from liber (free), gave nationalism its middle-class carriers: individual freedom, equality before the law, government by consent, and freedom of markets. In the fragmented German states the economic argument for unity was irresistible — a merchant in 1833 crossed eleven customs barriers, paid about 5 per cent at each and faced thirty currencies — and the Zollverein of 1834 abolished tariffs, cut currencies to two and built railways. Against this, the Congress of Vienna in 1815 restored a conservative order under Metternich, with Bourbon France, buffer states, Austrian control of northern Italy and a German confederation of 39 states. It could not last: the memory of the Revolution inspired liberals, producing the revolutions of 1830 and 1848, the latter bringing the Frankfurt Parliament of 831 members, which failed when Friedrich Wilhelm IV refused the crown and troops disbanded the assembly.

Germany was then unified by Prussia: Bismarck’s three wars over seven years with Austria, Denmark and France, and the proclamation of William I as Kaiser at Versailles on 18 January 1871, in a strong but authoritarian state dominated by the Junkers. Italy, divided into seven states, was unified through Mazzini’s Young Italy and Young Europe, Cavour’s diplomacy and alliance with France in 1859, and Garibaldi’s Red Shirts in the south in 1860, with Victor Emmanuel II proclaimed king in 1861. Britain took a different road — parliament, the Acts of Union of 1707 and 1801, a dominant English culture and the repression of Gaelic and Irish traditions — which is why its nationalism was unlike Europe’s.

The nation was visualised through allegory: Marianne with the red cap, tricolour and cockade, and Germania with the crown of oak leaves, sword, olive branch and black-red-gold flag. But by the last quarter of the century nationalism had narrowed into a creed of territory and power, and its most explosive site was the Balkans, where Ottoman disintegration, romantic nationalism, jealous states and great-power rivalry produced a series of wars and finally the First World War. Meanwhile colonised peoples turned nationalism against their rulers, and the idea that societies should be organised into nation-states became accepted as natural and universal.
